Skip next section Explosive-laden drone defused at Leipzig airport 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Explosive-laden drone defused at Leipzig airport German federal police specialists have defused a drone carrying an explosive device after an overnight security incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Officials said the detonator has been removed from an as-yet unidentified explosive device. Authorities say they are not ruling out a political motive, noting that the Leipzig/Halle airport in eastern Germany forms part of the country's critical infrastructure. The drone carrying the explosive device was found late on Wednesday by an airport employee on the southern runway, according to investigators. Another flying object later apparently collided with a cargo aircraft which was taxing on the ground. Minor damage was discovered after the aircraft landed in Hanover. Flight operations were initially halted completely after the drone was found. The northern runway was eventually reopened following a large-scale security sweep overnight, while the southern runway was due to remain closed on Wednesday for maintenance. Investigators said there was no danger to passengers or airport staff and that passenger flights were not affected. https://p.dw.com/p/5IKej Skip next section Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there A German court has ruled in favor of a woman who publicly criticized a restaurant after her dachshund ate mouse poison while she was dining there. The Frankfurt Higher Regional Court rejected the restaurant operator's attempt to stop her from describing the incident on Instagram and a review platform. The woman had visited the restaurant in the Rhine-Main region in spring 2026 with her dachshund, which was lying under a bench inside. The dog ate mouse bait from a pest-control bait station that had somehow been left accessible and later needed treatment at a veterinary clinic. That same day, the owner posted about the incident on her own Instagram account and on an account she ran for the dog. She described what happened as "shocking" and a "massive failure of safety and hygiene." The court found that readers would understand those remarks as referring to a single incident rather than suggesting the restaurant had permanent or structural hygiene problems. Judges said the woman was entitled to describe the fact that her dog had been able to reach poison as a "massive" failure, even if her wording was emotional and somewhat exaggerated. They also found that her inaccurate description of the harmful substance as "rat poison" was not so serious a mistake as to warrant restricting her comment. The statements were therefore protected expressions of opinion, it ruled. https://p.dw.com/p/5IKIn Skip next section German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell A court in Hamburg has handed down prison sentences of up to five years to eight alleged members and supporters of the far-right group "Letzte Verteidigungswelle" (Last Line of Defense). The Higher Regional Court convicted the young defendants on charges including membership in a terrorist organization and attempted murder. Prosecutors said the group had planned bomb and arson attacks targeting refugees and left-wing activists and had already carried out several attacks. Seven defendants received juvenile prison sentences ranging from two years and four months to five years. Another was given an 18-month suspended sentence. Three defendants were also convicted of leading the group. The presiding judge said they had aimed to "create chaos." Authorities dismantled the group in May last year after investigations spanning several German states. Prosecutors said members carried out an overnight arson attack on an occupied cultural center in Altdöbern in October 2024 and a pyrotechnic attack on a refugee accommodation center in Schmölln, Thuringia, in January 2025. No one was injured, although investigators said that was partly down to chance. The group had also been planning another attack on a refugee center in Senftenberg, Brandenburg. Several suspects were arrested in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg and Hesse. They were between 14 and 21 years old at the time. Because some defendants were minors, much of the trial was held behind closed doors. Read more about the story here . https://p.dw.com/p/5IJn7 Skip next section Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation Low water means that barges cannot carry as much cargo as they usually would Image: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO Persistently low water levels on the Rhine could temporarily push Germany's inflation rate up by as much as half a percentage point, economists have warned. Low water levels are forcing ships to carry much lighter loads, driving up the cost of transporting chemicals, energy supplies and other industrial goods. Traders said tanker and barge transport costs from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe have climbed to around €150-160 per ton, compared with about €45 at the end of June. "The German inflation rate could temporarily rise by up to half a percentage point as a result," Berenberg economist Felix Schmidt told the Reuters news agency. ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski also said shortages and disrupted deliveries could make a wide range of goods more expensive. "If ships can only be loaded to one-third of capacity or less, correspondingly more ships have to be used, or more expensive alternatives such as trucks or rail," Hamburg Commercial Bank chief economist Cyrus de la Rubia said. Economists also warned that the disruption could last for months. In previous years, Rhine water levels have often not recovered significantly until November. https://p.dw.com/p/5IJ4l Skip next section German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement 08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement A German employer group has sharply criticized calls to preserve the country's early retirement scheme as debate grows over a proposed overhaul of the pension system . A government-appointed pension commission presented 33 proposals in June, including abolishing the option of retiring without deductions for people who have paid into the system for particularly long periods. Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leadership initially said they wanted to implement the package as closely as possible to the commission's recommendations. However, several state premiers from both Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union and the SPD have since pushed back against parts of the plan, with particularly strong criticism coming from eastern Germany. Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper that Germany would not be able to protect jobs and remain competitive without reforming the welfare state. "I am stunned that central elements of the pension package are already being called into question before they have even been implemented," Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper. "Anyone who at the same time sticks to retirement from 63 is ignoring the shortage of skilled workers, demographic change and the economic situation," he said. He warned that watering down the reforms could squander "perhaps the last chance" to make the pension system sustainable as Germany's population ages. "A future-proof pension system needs more employment, more contributors and solid financing - not ever more promises at the expense of the younger generation," Kampeter said. Photograph: Yonhap/AFP/Getty Images US foreign policy Trump’s move to gut South Korea alliance is ‘inane, haphazard decision’, lawmakers say US president’s abrupt order to scale back joint exercises with Seoul is meant to ‘flatter’ North Korea’s dictator, top Democrat says US politics live – latest updates Joseph Gedeon in Washington Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.43 EDT Last modified on Mon 17 Aug 2026 13.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump’s move to gut Washington’s 73-year-old military alliance with Seoul has been called “inane” and “shortsighted” as lawmakers warned it risked strengthening Russia’s hand in Ukraine. The US president abruptly ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint exercises with South Korea just days after North Korea test-fired ballistic missiles, justifying the decision by citing his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong-Un, the nuclear-armed dictator such exercises exist to deter. Trump announced the order on social media, directing the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to scale back Ulchi Freedom Shield, an 11-day exercise due to run from 17 to 27 August involving about 18,000 South Korean troops rehearsing scenarios including missile strikes, drone incursions and cyber-attacks. Trump framed the decision as a courtesy to Kim, writing that the drills “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful”, despite North Korea’s continued missile testing and its expanding nuclear arsenal. Democrats in Congress said the move handed Kim a propaganda win for nothing, while an ally was left paying the price for a war in the Middle East it never agreed to fight. Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, called it “another inane, haphazard decision by President Trump and his chaotic administration”. “When President Trump cuts military exercises to flatter a dictator or punishes South Korea for declining to join a war he started, all of our allies – and adversaries – think that America’s commitments are negotiable,” Reed said in a statement, describing the move as punishing Korea “for no reason beyond Trump’s ego”. Reed’s warning was echoed by Mark Kelly of Arizona, who sits on the same committee, and argued that the drills were not symbolic but the basis of the alliance’s ability to function in a crisis. “North and South Korea are still technically at war,” Kelly said. “Our ability to help defend our ally against the North Koreans is because our forces are well trained and able to coordinate with the South Koreans. Hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake.” The alliance Trump is now unwinding dates to the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty signed after the Korean war armistice. Roughly 28,500 American troops remain stationed in South Korea, backed by a combined US-South Korean command structure and Washington’s pledge to extend its nuclear umbrella over Seoul. Despite Trump calling North Korea “unthreatening”, his own administration’s 2026 Annual Threat Assessment describes an “increasingly confident North Korean regime”, warning that its weapons of mass destruction, conventional forces and cyber operations threaten the US, South Korea and Japan. His former director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified in March that “North Korea’s ICBMs [intercontinental ballistic missiles] can already reach US soil”. Trump also tied his decision to the Iran war, saying he was unhappy that Seoul had declined to join the US military campaign against Iran, a campaign that has drained US missile stockpiles and, after Tehran shut the strait of Hormuz, helped push up prices at home . He acknowledged the two issues had little to do with one another, even as he punished Seoul over both. “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks’!” Trump wrote. Andy Kim, the New Jersey senator who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, said linking the exercises to that refusal exposed a troubling attitude toward a key partner. “Our alliance with the Republic of Korea is critical for US security and prosperity – and I am concerned that President Trump’s post today suggests a disregard for this relationship,” Kim said. “South Korea is an essential partner in peace and security in a part of the world filled with risk; we should treat them that way instead of venting frustration on social media.” It is not the first time Trump has treated the drills as a bargaining chip. After his 2018 summit with Kim in Singapore, he suspended major exercises outright, calling them costly and provocative, before they were quietly restored once nuclear diplomacy with Pyongyang broke down. The dispute comes as Seoul has spent much of the past year charting its own path on the Middle East. In February, South Korea’s government said it had “grave concern” over Israeli measures expanding control in the occupied West Bank and urged Israel to “reverse its decisions immediately”. In April, Seoul’s ambassador to the United Nations told the security council that any unilateral annexation of Palestinian territory “should be revoked”. Lee Jae-myung, the president of South Korea, has twice clashed publicly with Israel: in April over remarks he made comparing footage of an Israeli soldier’s treatment of a Palestinian man’s body to the Holocaust, and in May after two South Korean activists were detained on a Gaza-bound aid mission. Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, chimed in making the point that the butterfly effect of Trump’s decision would inadvertently benefit Russia. “South Korea has been a solid military ally for over 70 years that possesses exquisite military capabilities,” Tillis wrote on social media. “Reducing joint exercises with South Korea does nothing more than free up thousands of North Korea’s troops to support Putin’s systematic kidnapping, torture, rape and murder of innocent Ukrainian citizens.” Explore more on these topics US foreign policy Donald Trump South Korea US politics Trump administration Asia Pacific US national security news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://therightscoop.com/breaking-a-pol.text: Share Twitter/X Facebook Truth Social Telegram Copy Link There’s a political coup underway in Poland right now and it centers around the country’s Constitutional Tribunal. This is not a military coup. Similar to our Supreme Court, it rules on whether laws passed by parliament and actions by the government or president comply with the constitution, and it can strike laws down. It all has to do with a political war between the country’s Prime Minister, Donald Tusk, and the Polish President Karol Nawrocki. Here’s an AI summary of what is happening. Because honestly, I’m still trying to wrap my brain around it all. Being an outsider, it’s confusing: The flashpoint is Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, its top court. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government has been electing new judges to it; President Karol Nawrocki, aligned with the opposition PiS, refuses to swear several of them in. Tusk says he’s legally required to; Nawrocki says the appointments are illegitimate. Today, the government-backed judges moved into the Tribunal building, installed Anna Korwin-Piotrowska as its head, and suspended the sitting president, Bogdan Święczkowski. Święczkowski — holed up and refusing to recognize them — called it a “coup d’état,” and PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński said Poland is becoming a “police state.” Tusk’s side calls it restoring the rule of law after years of PiS packing the court. Nawrocki was on his way to Senegal but turned his plane around to head back and deal with the situation. To go deeper , this is from the BBC explaining the backstory: The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation. Leading European courts – the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union – subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament. The European courts ruled Poland’s Constitutional Court was no longer an “independent and impartial tribunal”, and Tusk’s government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal’s rulings. Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts. This is hugely important, but like I said, it’s not a military coup. The visuals of riot police and protesters is all about the high court and what’s going on inside.
